title: Trump’s Putin Overtures Deserve Criticism. But Outrage Won’t End the Ukraine War. | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Thomas Graham argues the West should stop demanding a 'just peace' in Ukraine and aim for an achievable, imperfect one: Russia keeps most seized land, sanctions are at diminishing returns, and Cold War-style normalization with Russia is both inevitable and desirable.

insights.claim: A Russia-Ukraine settlement will not be just: Russia will retain most of the Ukrainian land it has seized and Ukraine can at best withhold legal recognition.
insights.so_what: Position for a frozen-line outcome rather than a Ukrainian reconquest.
insights.locator: Ukraine and its Western backers continue to insist
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: Western policy should target an achievable peace that preserves Ukrainian sovereignty on as much of its 1991 territory as possible and keeps European integration, short of NATO membership, on track.
insights.so_what: Defines the realistic end-state for European security architecture.
insights.locator: In part, that would entail preserving
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: Reaching that peace requires continued strong Western supply of weapons and intelligence to Ukraine to thwart Russian advances and defend against aerial bombardment.
insights.so_what: Leverage in talks rests on sustained military support.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: Wars where neither side wins decisively end in messy compromises, and countries sharing a continent must eventually coexist.
insights.so_what: Frames the ceasefire as compromise, not victory.
insights.quote: wars in which neither side achieves a decisive victory end in messy compromises
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: After four and a half years, sanctions have been much less consequential than promised and have probably long since reached diminishing returns.
insights.so_what: Do not assume added sanctions will materially pressure Russia.
insights.locator: Sanctions do have a role to play
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: Normalization with Russia should be understood as Cold War-style channels of communication and habits of consultation that avert crises, not a return to broad cooperation, and it can coexist with fundamental rivalry.
insights.so_what: Reframes US engagement as crisis management rather than reward.
insights.locator: This is far too positive and generous
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: Ukrainian and European leaders categorically reject US talk of normalization because they see it as rewarding an unrepentant Russia, an argument Graham says misses the point.
insights.so_what: Signals a transatlantic split on Russia policy.
insights.locator: Ukrainian and European leaders have categorically rejected this
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: In the initial post-conflict years Europe and Ukraine will organize their security against Russia with a credible deterrent force, but cost pressure will likely lead to arms control agreements and growing societal interaction.
insights.so_what: Medium-term European defense spending is sustained, then arms control returns.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: Europe still needs access to Russian energy resources, if not to the excess of earlier years, to diversify suppliers and lower prices.
insights.so_what: Implies partial return of Russian energy to European supply mix after settlement.
insights.locator: Russia and Europe, including Ukraine, remain natural commercial partners
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: Steve Witkoff met Putin for the ninth time in St. Petersburg days after the White House eased sanctions on Russian diesel, and had met Zelenskyy in Oslo the day before amid a dispute over military aid, intelligence sharing and Starshield access.
insights.so_what: Evidence of US tilt toward accommodation with Russia and strain with Kyiv.
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham

insights.claim: Outrage at Trump's accommodation of Putin is justifiable but has not clarified the hard choices of what can be achieved in the short term.
insights.so_what: Argues for assessing diplomacy against feasibility, not rhetoric.
insights.quote: rhetoric substitutes for a hard-nosed assessment
insights.speaker: Thomas Graham
